least-squares-regression-s1.title: Computer output: car weight and fuel economy
least-squares-regression-s1.text: For a random sample of 30 car models, a magazine regresses highway fuel economy (miles per gallon) on weight (thousands of pounds). Part of the output is below. (Invented data.)

table.caption: Regression of fuel economy (mpg) on weight (1,000 lb)

least-squares-regression-s2.title: Practice and free throws, with one unusual player
least-squares-regression-s2.text: A coach records practice hours per week and free throw percentage for 11 players. One player practices 16 hours a week and makes 58% of free throws. (Invented data.)

plot.label: Scatterplot of 11 players: ten with 2 to 8 practice hours and 52 to 70 percent rising steeply, and one at 16 hours and 58 percent far to the right, with the least-squares line for all 11 players

least-squares-regression-s3.title: Summary statistics for ten players
least-squares-regression-s3.text: For the ten players who practice 2 to 8 hours a week, the coach computes these summaries of practice hours ($x$) and free throw percentage ($y$). The scatterplot is linear with no unusual points. (Invented data.)

items.q: Which is the correct interpretation of the slope?

why.correct: Slope in context with "predicted" and the units of $x$.
options: Right: the slope is the predicted change in $y$ per one-unit increase in $x$, and the unit of $x$ here is 1,000 pounds.
The slope describes predicted values, not an exact change for each car.
That mixes up the slope and the intercept, and a weight of 0 is not sensible.
Weight is in thousands of pounds, so one unit of $x$ is 1,000 pounds.
For each extra 1,000 lb, predicted fuel economy drops by about 6.25 mpg
For each additional 1,000 pounds, each car loses exactly 6.25 mpg
A car that weighs 0 pounds is predicted to get 6.25 mpg
For each additional pound of weight, the predicted fuel economy decreases by about 6.25 mpg

items.q: Which is the correct interpretation of R-Sq = 76.4%?

why.correct: $r^2$: "About [r squared]% of the variation in [y] is accounted for by the linear model using [x]."
options: Right: $r^2$ is the fraction of the variation in $y$ explained by the line.
$r^2$ measures how much variation the line accounts for, not cause.
$r^2$ is not a share of cars; predictions are rarely exactly right.
The correlation is $r = -\sqrt{0.764} = -0.874$, negative because the slope is negative.
About 76.4% of the variation in fuel economy is accounted for by the linear model using weight
Weight causes about 76.4% of the variation in a car's fuel economy
About 76.4% of the cars in the sample have fuel economy the line predicts correctly
The correlation between weight and fuel economy for these 30 car models is 0.764

items.q: Which is the correct interpretation of S = 2.81?

why.correct: $s$: "The actual [y] typically differs from the predicted [y] by about $s$ [units]."
options: Right: $s$, the standard deviation of the residuals, is the typical size of a prediction error, in the units of $y$.
That would be a slope; the slope here is $-6.25$.
The unexplained share is $100\% - 76.4\% = 23.6\%$; $s$ is in mpg, not a percent.
$s$ measures scatter around the line in $y$ units, not the spread of $x$.
A car's actual mpg is typically about 2.81 mpg away from its predicted mpg
The predicted fuel economy changes by about 2.81 mpg for each additional 1,000 pounds
About 2.81% of the variation in fuel economy is left unexplained
The cars' weights typically differ from their mean weight by about 2.81 thousand pounds

items.q: How is the player at 16 hours best described?

why.correct: High leverage: an extreme $x$ value. Influential: removing it changes the line a lot.
options: Its $x$ value, 16, is twice the next largest, which makes it unusual.
The line is pulled close to it, so its residual is not very large; that is what influence looks like.
Its 58% is ordinary on its own, but at 16 hours it is far from the others' $x$ values, so it moves the line a lot.
Right: far from $\bar{x}$ gives high leverage, and removing it changes the slope a lot.
A typical point, since it lies inside the range of $y$ values
A point with a large residual that the line passes far from
An outlier with no effect on the line, since its percentage is ordinary
High leverage and influential: extreme $x$, and it pulls the line

items.q: With all 11 players the least-squares slope is about 0.49. What happens to the slope if the 16-hour player is removed?

why.correct: Removing an influential point changes the slope substantially.
options: The other ten points rise steeply; the slope without the point is positive and large.
The unusual point is below where the trend of the others would put it, so removing it makes the line steeper, not flatter.
A point with high leverage can change the slope a great deal, as here.
Right: technology gives $b = 2.92$ for the other ten players. The one point had flattened the line.
It becomes negative
It decreases to about 0.24
It stays about 0.49, since one point out of 11 is small
It increases to about 2.92

items.q: With all 11 players, $r = 0.32$. Without the 16-hour player, $r = 0.97$. What does this show?

why.correct: Unusual points can change $r$ and the slope; analyze with and without them.
options: Among the ten typical players the association is strong; the weak $r$ is caused by one point.
Report the point and the analysis with and without it; do not delete data without a reason.
Right: correlation is not resistant; one high-leverage point weakened it from 0.97 to 0.32.
The change from 0.97 to 0.32 shows the opposite.
Practice has little to do with free throws for these players
The 16-hour player should be deleted from any report
One point hides a strong linear link among the other ten
Correlation is resistant to unusual points

items.q: Write the expression for the slope of the least-squares line, $b = r\frac{s_y}{s_x}$, with the values substituted, then evaluate it.

mistakes.why: The fraction is upside down: $b = r\frac{s_y}{s_x}$, the response's SD over the explanatory variable's SD.
That leaves out $r$. The slope is $r$ times the ratio of standard deviations.

items.q: The least-squares line passes through $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$. Using the slope from the data, $b = 2.917$, what is the intercept $a$? Give two decimal places.

mistakes.why: That adds $b\bar{x}$. Since $\bar{y} = a + b\bar{x}$, subtract: $a = \bar{y} - b\bar{x}$.
That is $\bar{y}$, the predicted value at $\bar{x} = 5$, not at $x = 0$.

items.q: What is $r^2$ for these ten players? Give three decimal places.

mistakes.why: That is $r$. Square it to get the coefficient of determination.

items.q: A player practices exactly 5 hours a week, the mean. What free throw percentage does the least-squares line predict?

options: At $x = \bar{x}$ the prediction is exactly $\bar{y}$.
The intercept is the prediction at 0 hours, not at 5.
The prediction is in percent made, the $y$ variable.
Right: the least-squares line always passes through $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$.
About 64.3%, one SD of $x$ above the mean of $y$
46.8%, the intercept
5%, the mean of $x$
61.4%, the mean of $y$

items.q: A player 1 standard deviation above the mean in practice hours (7 hours) is predicted to be how far above the mean in free throw percentage?

why.correct: $b = r\frac{s_y}{s_x}$: one $s_x$ step in $x$ gives $r \cdot s_y$ in $\hat{y}$.
options: 2.917 is the slope in percentage points per hour, not in standard deviations.
One SD in $x$ gives $r$ SDs in $y$, not 2.
Right: in standard units the line predicts $r$ SDs of $y$ for each SD of $x$: $0.966(6.04) = 5.8$.
Only if $r = 1$. With $r = 0.966$, predictions regress slightly toward the mean.
2.917 standard deviations
2 standard deviations, 12.08 points
About 0.966 standard deviations, about 5.8 points
Exactly 1 standard deviation, 6.04 points, as $x$ moved 1 SD

items.q: What makes the least-squares regression line "least squares"?

options: Right: among all lines, it gives the smallest $\sum (y - \hat{y})^2$.
It may pass through none of the points.
No line can make every residual small; it minimizes the sum of their squares.
The slope is whatever minimizes the squared residuals.
It minimizes the sum of the squared residuals
It passes through as many data points as possible
It makes each residual as small as possible
It has the smallest possible slope

items.q: For a regression with negative slope, $r^2 = 0.81$. What is the correlation?

why.correct: $r$ has the sign of $b$ and size $\sqrt{r^2}$.
options: That squares 0.81 again.
Take the square root of $r^2$.
The square root has two signs; the negative slope means $r$ is negative.
Right: $r = \pm\sqrt{0.81} = \pm 0.9$, and it takes the sign of the slope.

items.q: A line predicts exam score from hours studied for 40 students, with $r^2 = 0.64$. Interpret $r^2$ in context.

why.correct: $r^2$: the share of the variation in $y$ accounted for by the line.

amount.label: Amount
options: About 64% of the variation in exam score
About 64% of the students' exam scores
About 80% of the variation in exam score

why.1: $r^2$ is about variation in $y$, not a share of students.
why.2: 80% is $r$ as a percent; the question gives $r^2$.

cause.label: Explained by
options: is accounted for by the linear model using hours studied.
is caused by hours studied.
is predicted exactly by the line.

why.2: Predictions are not exact; there is still unexplained variation.

conclude.model: About 64% of the variation in exam score is accounted for by the linear model using hours studied.

items.q: A point has an $x$ value near $\bar{x}$ but a $y$ value far above the rest of the data. What does it change most?

why.correct: Outlier in $y$ near $\bar{x}$: big residual, little leverage.
options: A point above the middle of the data lifts the line up; it does not flip its direction.
Right: near $\bar{x}$ it has little leverage, so the slope hardly moves, but its large residual adds scatter.
A point near $\bar{x}$ has low leverage on the slope; its big residual does affect $s$ and $r$.
A large residual affects $s$, $r$ and $r^2$, and shifts the intercept a little.
It makes the slope negative
It raises $s$ and lowers $r$, but barely changes the slope
It changes the slope a lot, but leaves $s$ about the same
It has no effect on the line or its summaries

items.q: A line predicts the weight of a fish (grams) from its length (cm), with $s = 42$. What are the units of $s$?

options: $s$ measures vertical gaps, in units of the response.
$r^2$ is a percent; $s$ is in grams.
Right: $s$ is a typical residual, so it has the units of $y$.
That is the unit of the slope.
Centimeters
Percent
Grams
Grams per centimeter
